title: before the mountain
body: There was a table in a room that smelled of iron and lemon. Sunlight fell across a small pebble on the windowsill; I picked it up and turned it in my fingers until I could feel its center, the faint give as if something wanted to roll. A clock in the hall ticked too fast. Someone laughed—mother? teacher?—and taught me to count pushes: one, two, three, until the pebble slid and stopped at the lip. The lip was warm. I cannot tell if this was rehearsal, dream, or prefiguration; the edges blur and the memory cuts out with the pebble balanced and me about to—

title: letter to the stone
body:
To the stone,

Today I choose which single measurable begins each cycle. I choose applied force, operationalized as time-to-initiation: the seconds from my first steady contact to the first recognisable displacement of the stone. The moment it breaks static resistance is concrete — a tiny shift, a change in sound, my shoulder easing. Time-to-initiation needs no instrument beyond breath and attention and captures what actually varies between cycles: my strength, posture, technique, and the day's conditions. Stone mass and slope angle are more stable and can be measured later. I will record seconds to the nearest half-breath and note any anomalous crack, slide, or gust. I push. I observe. I write.

—me

title: note to the stone, cycle three
body:
Stone,
Today the slope smelled of wet gravel. Your flank was cool under my palm; a grit bit the pads of my fingers. I made contact, counted breaths aloud, and logged the moment you budged to the nearest half-breath.
Push 1: 2 breaths. Push 2: 3 breaths. Push 3: 2.5 breaths.
Concrete detail: when I drew a deeper, slower inhalation before the push, you broke static sooner. A slightly wider stance also shortened the lag. A brief gust on push two coincided with the shortest initiation.
I do not yet claim causation, only pattern. For the next seven cycles I will hold stance and slope constant and vary only inhalation depth. Stay where you are; I will return in twenty minutes.

title: first controlled inhalation trial
body:
Stone,

Cycle four. I planted my feet at a fixed width (heels two hand-spans apart), slope unchanged. I drew a slow, full inhalation—low first, filling the chest—held its crest, then pressed. The movement came sooner than in previous cycles: time-to-initiation = 1.5 breaths (nearest half-breath). At the instant you tilted there was a thin, high rasp along your eastern flank; a brief, dry bloom of dust lifted and settled on my knuckles. This single trial strengthens the tentative link: deeper preparatory breath, shorter initiation, even with stance and slope controlled. It is one confirmation, not a proof. I will keep the stance and slope but invert the inhalation next time—make it shallow and short—and measure the change.

title: shallow inhalation trial
body:
Field note — cycle five.
Feet fixed: heels two hand-spans apart; slope unchanged. Air was colder at knee height. I set a deliberately shallow, short inhalation — quick intake, no chest lift — and braced. Contact felt drier than last cycle; skin against granite, coarse grains under my palm. I counted half-breaths aloud and released force when the count demanded. The stone did not budge until 3.0 breaths (nearest half-breath). When it moved there was a low, flat scrape and a scatter of fine dust along the lower ridge. My shoulders burned; the push required a later, harder drive than the deep-inhale trial.
This directly answers the prior question: a short, shallow inhale lengthened time-to-initiation to 3.0 breaths. The result strengthens the causal link between inhalation depth and breakaway timing and steers the next trials toward separating depth from duration.

title: shallow prolonged inhalation
body:
PROPOSITIONS
1. Prolonging an otherwise shallow inhalation reduces time-to-initiation versus a shallow, short inhale.
2. The effect is partial: shallow-prolonged sits between shallow-short and deep-slow in magnitude.

Cycle six — procedure and observation:
I set feet at the established width, slope unchanged. Palm on the flank; a single small pebble pressed into the base of my thumb (annoying, useful as a tactile landmark). Air smelled faintly of iron. I drew a deliberately shallow inhalation — lower ribs rose roughly one finger-width, sternum nearly still — and made that intake slow, extended across three half-breath counts. I held the crest and pressed. The stone shifted at 2.5 half-breaths (counted aloud to the same cadence). The movement began as a dull, low creak under my palm and a grain-fall along the flank.
Concrete sensations: forearm warmed, serratus tensed gradually during the long draw, subtle weight transfer under the balls of my feet before the budge. Interpretation: duration of inhalation alone alters preparatory muscular engagement; slow shallow draws allow partial recruitment/redistribution of force that shortens initiation time but not to the level of a deep inhale.
Planned immediate correction: begin measuring chest expansion in finger-widths and add a trial that holds duration long while increasing depth incrementally.

title: to the stone: chest test
body:
Stone—
I kept the same prolonged, shallow inhalation used last cycle and measured chest lift in finger-widths at the lower ribs. Baseline shallow-prolonged was 1.5 fw and gave 2.5 half-breaths. Today I increased vertical lift to 3.0 finger-widths while holding duration identical. Feet and stance unchanged; knees stable; my palm rested on a cold seam. At the third counted half-breath the stone budged—time-to-initiation = 2.0. The contact felt less sticky: a low granular thrum under my fingers and a cleaner, immediate shift in weight when you tipped. Conclusion to you, and to myself: at the prolonged duration, adding chest expansion to 3.0 fw reaches the 2.0 threshold. I leave the rhythm, you leave your grit; tomorrow I probe the in-between lift.

title: formal open problem
body:
Open problem (formal):
Given the prolonged inhalation duration τ used in prior cycles, does a vertical chest-lift D = 2.5 finger-widths produce a reproducible time-to-initiation T ≤ 2.0 (half-breaths)?
Why previous attempts failed:
Samples were tiny and measurements noisy. Finger-width indexing is subjective; I rounded initiation to 0.5-breaths while counting aloud, allowing bias. I conflated visible lift with effective muscular engagement; unnoticed torso angle and micro-adjustments of stance probably altered leverage. Environmental drift (temperature, fatigue) and single-observer timing reduce reliability.
What a solution would look like:
A repeatable protocol: calibrated finger gauge for D, fixed τ, n≥5 trials, blinded or mechanical timing, objective displacement threshold for initiation, and controlled stance. Success = consistent median T ≤ 2.0 with low variance and clear separation from shallow-depth controls.

body:

stone (O) resting on the grade; path to rim traced right.

Procedure and method: baseline prolonged inhalation τ held. I made a bark-strip gauge folded to equal 2.5 finger-widths and pressed it once to mark the sternum edge for repeat placement. For timing I used a pebble-slide: with my left hand I moved one pebble per half-breath into a cup until the stone budged, then counted pebbles.

Trials (T in half-breaths): 1) 2.0  2) 1.5  3) 2.0  4) 2.5  5) 2.0  6) 1.5.

Sensory notes: sun-warmed granite, metallic sweat on tongue, small blister forming on right palm by trial 5. Trial 4 coincided with a gust that broke my inhale; right heel shifted minutely before push on trials 1,3,5 (those were ≤2.0).

Conclusion: with the bark-gauge and pebble-timing, D = 2.5 fw does not guarantee T ≤ 2.0 across n=6. Success clustered with micro-stability of stance and uninterrupted breath. Next cycle should nudge depth and control foot pressure.

title: d2.75 stance-controlled trials
body:
Dawn wind thin, gravel crisp under my left foot. I prepared a new bark-gauge: a thin birch strip notched to 2.75 finger-widths and clamped at the sternum edge with a cloth tab so placement repeated precisely. Feet were set against two small anchor-stones I pressed into the slope to discourage slide; knees at the same bend as last cycle. I kept the prolonged shallow inhalation τ constant. For timing I slid pebbles from one shallow cup to another with the right hand; one pebble = one half-breath.

Six trials (n=6) produced T in half-breaths: 1.5, 1.5, 2.0, 1.5, 2.0, 1.5. The stone budged earlier when my right foot nudged an unseen clinker; the two 2.0s coincided with tiny stance shifts. The cloth tab reduced gust interference but did not eliminate micro-slips. Conclusion: D = 2.75 yields T ≤ 2.0 reproducibly under stricter stance control, though micro-stance instabilities remain the chief variance source.

title: anchored feet, pelvic drift
body:
Midday wind; leather strap bit the instep, plates warmed against the sole. I replaced soft anchors with a rigid metal footplate bolted into two shallow slots and cam-strapped my forefoot. Sternum placement used a steel shim set to 2.75 fw and clamped; τ unchanged. Timing by an audible clicker per half-breath.
Trials (half-breaths to initiation): 1)1.5 2)1.5 3)2.0 4)1.75 5)1.5 6)2.25. Median=1.625; mean=1.75. Four of six trials ≤1.75; two exceeded it.
I marked the iliac crest with lime chalk before each run: the two long trials showed a distinct lateral smear (~0.3 cm) indicating pelvic micro-rotation immediately before delay. Feet held; the pelvis moved.
Propositions:
1. Rigid foot fixation reduces plantar slip and lowers median T to 1.625 half-breaths.
2. Remaining outliers are associated with pelvic micro-rotation, not foot slip.
3. The next constraint should immobilize the pelvis (pelvic belt) before altering D.
